title: Options to stop political dynasties
primary_topics: Four options for enforcing the constitutional anti-dynasty provision (Art. II Sec. 26): legislative, judicial/quasi-judicial, sovereign (peoples initiative), and political
Why the legislative, judicial, and sovereign options are legally untenable or practically foreclosed at this time
Political action -- voting down dynasty candidates in 2013 elections -- as the most doable option under present circumstances
sub_topics: Art. II Sec. 26: The state shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service, and prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law
25 years of legislative inaction -- legislators with relatives in office have no incentive to pass an enabling law
Judicial petitions to compel Comelec to enforce the ban -- untenable because Comelec cannot legislate without an enabling law
Mandamus to compel Congress to pass enabling law -- iffy because the duty is not purely ministerial
Term limits as self-executory (contrast with dynasty ban): courts can disqualify candidates using bare constitutional limits

2013 elections as a referendum on dynasties -- if people vote down dynasty candidates, new Congress will enact enabling law

stances.claim: The legislative option is the no-brainer solution but practically foreclosed because legislators with relatives in office have no incentive -- 25 years of inaction confirm this.

Judicial and quasi-judicial options are legally untenable: the dynasty ban is not self-executory unlike term limits, the Comelec cannot legislate without an enabling law, and courts cannot compel discretionary legislative acts via mandamus.

The peoples initiative for an anti-dynasty law faces the Lambino v. Comelec bar by analogy: an anti-dynasty law is too controversial and complex for a simple initiative; it requires a deliberative body with recorded proceedings.
stances.rhetorical_move: Lambino-analogy extension to block the sovereign option

stances.claim: The political option -- voting down dynasty candidates in 2013, forming movements like KAPAL, using social media -- is most doable and if successful would produce a Congress with the mandate to enact the enabling law.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes four options for enforcing the 25-year-old unenforced constitutional anti-dynasty provision (Art. II Sec. 26). The legislative option is the 'no-brainer' but practically foreclosed because legislators with relatives in office have no incentive. Judicial and quasi-judicial options -- petitions to compel the Comelec to deny certificates of candidacy, or mandamus against Congress -- are legally untenable: the Comelec cannot legislate without an enabling law, the dynasty ban is not self-executory (unlike term limits), and mandamus cannot compel a discretionary legislative act. Comelec Chair Brillantes's proposed people's initiative faces the Lambino v. Comelec bar by analogy: a controversial anti-dynasty law requires a deliberative body with recorded proceedings, not a simple initiative process. That leaves political action -- forming movements like KAPAL (Kamag-anak sa Politika Aayawan Lahat), using social media as Obama successfully did, and letting the 2013 elections serve as a referendum. If voters demonstrably reject dynasty candidates, the new Congress will have the mandate to finally enact the enabling law.
